newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Short end only glimmer in French curve.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Short end only glimmer in French curve.

text.p: French bonds will continue in a state of suspended animation with little to entice international investors except some slight outperformance at the front end of the curve, analysts said on Thursday.
Politics and supply concerns threaten to spook the long end but the front end could still benefit from interest rate easing and steepening ahead of European economic union, analysts said.
"If you're looking for movement somewhere on the curve it will probably be there," said Alison Cottrell, international economist at PaineWebber in London.
Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW here said, "That's quite a good trade because then you're being quite defensive and you've got the steeping trade on."

Yields on benchmark 10-year French bonds (OATs) collided with their German counterparts at the beginning of May and have been largely stuck there ever since. At 1215 GMT, the OAT/Bund gap was at minus one basis point.
The gap risks widening in the months ahead, however with talk of a cabinet reshuffle expected to start to gnaw at the French market, analysts said.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe has sunk to new lows in opinion polls, as he takes the brunt of unhappiness over the unpleasant effects of austerity policies aimed at whipping France into fiscal shape for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
There has even been talk of Juppe losing his post but official sources said on Wednesday he would stay on.
"If you're looking over the next few months then the political risk is not going to go away and that will probably weigh on the long end," said Cotterell.

Audrey Child-Freeman, French economist at I.D.E.A. in London said however, political concerns should not last. "France has committed itself to being part of EMU so there is no way we would see an u-turn in terms of economy policy," she said.
Reed at BZW said further ahead in 1997, the French market would also be depressed by a huge wave of supply.
France's medium and long term borrowing needs are set to rise to 689.7 billion francs in 1997 from 528.9 billion this year, according to a parliamentary finance committee in October.
"That's pretty high," said Reed, adding it was around eight percent of GDP. "Domestic demand may take up quite a lot of it but probably not all. Who's going to take up the slack?."
Any signs that EMU would not go ahead as planned in 1999 would also tend to weigh on the long end, she said.
"You could quite easily see the spread going back up into positive territory and pushing up to plus 20 or 25 basis points. If it really looked bad it could look a lot worse than than."
But for the most part, Reed said enthusiasm over EMU would continue to buoy the market, particularly at the short end.

"While everything seems to be all go with EMU...we would argue for the front end steepening a bit more to converge completely with Germany," Reed said. The spread between two-year French and German paper is currently at 22 basis points.
But the main factor which would nudge short-end yields lower was further trimming in French interest rates, analysts said.

"We don't seen a great deal of margin for them to ease further but they will continue little by little," Child-Freeman said. She expects around another 20 basis points off the 3.20 percent intervention rate in chunks of five basis points each.
But analysts said the speed of the cuts would be largely determined by the health of the franc, which was expected to benefit from talk to bolster the dollar.
"Given that all central banks concerned cannot speak now without trying to talk the dollar up there is a sensitivty in keeping dollar/mark stable," Cotterell said.

"When dollar/mark is stable then you will probably find the crosses continue to benefit against the mark which allows them to trim. That will help the whole rate cutting scenario to be taken forward a little bit more," she said.
